subject: chemistry
title: Intermolecular forces
summary: The types of attraction between particles — ion–dipole, dipole–dipole, hydrogen bonding and London dispersion — and how they explain boiling point, viscosity, surface tension and solubility.
body:
Intermolecular forces are the attractions between separate particles, as opposed to the bonds holding atoms together inside a molecule. They decide whether a substance is a gas, liquid or solid at room temperature, why water beads on a waxed car, why honey pours slowly and why oil and water do not mix. In CHM1011 you are expected not just to name these forces but to rank them, explain their origin in terms of electron distribution and use them to predict physical properties.

## Key ideas

### Intra- versus intermolecular

**Intramolecular forces** (covalent, ionic and metallic bonds) hold atoms together within a molecule or lattice; typical covalent bond energies are a few hundred kJ mol⁻¹. **Intermolecular forces** act between molecules and are much weaker, typically about 0.1–40 kJ mol⁻¹. When water boils, O–H covalent bonds are not broken: the molecules simply separate. That is why the enthalpy of vaporisation of water (40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 100 °C) is far smaller than the energy needed to break its two O–H bonds (about 920 kJ mol⁻¹).

All intermolecular forces are electrostatic: partial or full charges attract opposite charges. Their strength depends on the size of the charges and how close they can get.

### Polarity and dipole moments

A bond is polar when the atoms differ in **electronegativity**, the ability of an atom in a bond to attract shared electrons. The more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge (δ−). A molecule has a permanent **dipole moment**, μ, if its bond dipoles do not cancel; μ = Qr (charge × separation), measured in debye (1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m). Molecular shape matters: CO₂ has polar C=O bonds but is linear, so the dipoles cancel and μ = 0; H₂O is bent, so μ ≈ 1.85 D.

### Ion–dipole forces

An **ion–dipole force** is the attraction between an ion and the oppositely charged end of a polar molecule. It is the strongest of the intermolecular forces listed here and drives the dissolving of ionic salts in water: Na⁺ is surrounded by water molecules pointing their δ− oxygen towards it, while Cl⁻ attracts the δ+ hydrogens. This surrounding is called **hydration**. Ion–dipole attraction is stronger for small, highly charged ions (high **charge density**), which is why Mg²⁺ has a much more exothermic hydration enthalpy than Na⁺.

### Dipole–dipole forces

**Dipole–dipole forces** arise between polar molecules: the δ+ end of one molecule attracts the δ− end of a neighbour. Compare propane (C₃H₈, non-polar, M = 44, b.p. −42 °C) with ethanal (CH₃CHO, polar, M = 44, b.p. 20 °C): with similar size and shape, the dipole raises the boiling point by over 60 °C.

### Hydrogen bonding

A **hydrogen bond** is an especially strong dipole–dipole attraction between an H atom covalently bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on another N, O or F atom. It is strong for three reasons: the N–H, O–H and F–H bonds are very polar; H has no inner electrons, so its nucleus is almost exposed; and the small size of H lets the lone pair approach very closely. Hydrogen bonds are typically 10–40 kJ mol⁻¹ and strongest when X–H···Y is near linear.

The effect shows clearly in the group 16 hydrides. H₂S, H₂Se and H₂Te boil at −60, −41 and −2 °C, rising with size. Extrapolating, H₂O "should" boil near −80 °C, but it actually boils at 100 °C. Each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds (two through its H atoms, two through its lone pairs), giving an extended network.

### London dispersion forces and polarisability

**London dispersion forces** act between all particles, polar or not. At any instant, the electron cloud of a molecule may be unevenly distributed, creating an **instantaneous dipole**. This distorts the electron cloud of a neighbour, creating an **induced dipole**, and the two attract. The ease with which an electron cloud is distorted is its **polarisability**. Polarisability increases with:

- **Number of electrons and size** — larger electron clouds held further from the nucleus are more easily distorted. Halogens show this: F₂ (gas), Cl₂ (gas), Br₂ (liquid), I₂ (solid) at room temperature.
- **Surface area of contact (shape)** — long, straight molecules touch over a larger area than compact, branched ones. Pentane (b.p. 36 °C) boils higher than its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane (b.p. 10 °C), though both are C₅H₁₂.

A key exam idea is that dispersion forces are often the *largest* contribution for big molecules, even polar ones. HCl (b.p. −85 °C) is more polar than HI (b.p. −35 °C), yet HI boils higher because its much larger, more polarisable electron cloud gives stronger dispersion forces.

### Ranking forces and predicting properties

When comparing substances, first identify all forces present, then compare. A useful order for molecules of similar size is: ion–dipole > hydrogen bonding > dipole–dipole > dispersion. For molecules of very different size, dispersion can outweigh the others.

| Property | Effect of stronger intermolecular forces | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Boiling point | Higher | More energy is needed to separate molecules into the gas |
| Enthalpy of vaporisation | Larger | Same reason |
| Vapour pressure | Lower | Fewer molecules have enough energy to escape the surface |
| Viscosity | Higher | Molecules resist sliding past each other |
| Surface tension | Higher | Surface molecules are pulled inwards more strongly |

**Viscosity** is a liquid's resistance to flow. It increases with intermolecular forces and with molecular length (long chains tangle), and decreases with temperature. Glycerol, with three OH groups per molecule, is far more viscous than ethanol, which has one.

**Surface tension** is the energy needed to increase a liquid's surface area. Molecules at the surface have no neighbours above them, so they experience a net inward pull; the liquid minimises its surface, which is why droplets are spherical. Water's surface tension is unusually high for a small molecule because of hydrogen bonding.

### Solubility: "like dissolves like"

Dissolving requires breaking solute–solute and solvent–solvent attractions and forming solute–solvent attractions. A solute dissolves well when the new attractions are comparable in strength to those broken (entropy of mixing then tips the balance). Hence polar and ionic solutes tend to dissolve in polar solvents, and non-polar solutes in non-polar solvents. Hexane does not dissolve in water not because hexane and water repel, but because water molecules would lose hydrogen bonds to each other without gaining anything comparable from hexane. In a homologous series of alcohols, solubility in water falls as the non-polar hydrocarbon chain lengthens: methanol, ethanol and propanol are fully miscible, but hexan-1-ol is only slightly soluble.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: ranking boiling points

Rank CH₄, CH₃OH, CH₃Cl and C₂H₆ in order of increasing boiling point and justify.

**Step 1 – identify forces.**
- CH₄ (M = 16, 10 electrons): non-polar; dispersion only.
- C₂H₆ (M = 30, 18 electrons): non-polar; dispersion only, but larger than CH₄.
- CH₃Cl (M = 50.5, 26 electrons): polar; dipole–dipole plus significant dispersion.
- CH₃OH (M = 32, 18 electrons): polar with O–H; hydrogen bonding, dipole–dipole and dispersion.

**Step 2 – compare.** CH₄ < C₂H₆ because ethane has more electrons and greater polarisability. CH₃Cl has both more electrons than ethane and a permanent dipole. CH₃OH is smaller than CH₃Cl but hydrogen bonds.

**Answer:** CH₄ (−162 °C) < C₂H₆ (−89 °C) < CH₃Cl (−24 °C) < CH₃OH (65 °C). Here hydrogen bonding outweighs the larger dispersion forces of CH₃Cl.

### Example 2: estimating bond polarity from dipole moments

HCl has μ = 1.08 D and a bond length of 127 pm. Estimate the partial charge on each atom as a fraction of the electron charge, e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and compare with HF (μ = 1.82 D, 91.7 pm).

**Formula:** μ = Qr, so Q = μ / r.

**HCl:** μ = 1.08 × 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m = 3.603 × 10⁻³⁰ C m
Q = 3.603 × 10⁻³⁰ C m / 1.27 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 2.837 × 10⁻²⁰ C
Q/e = 2.837 × 10⁻²⁰ / 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ = **0.177**, so roughly δ = ±0.18.

**HF:** μ = 1.82 × 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ = 6.072 × 10⁻³⁰ C m
Q = 6.072 × 10⁻³⁰ / 9.17 × 10⁻¹¹ = 6.621 × 10⁻²⁰ C; Q/e = **0.413**, so δ ≈ ±0.41.

**Interpretation:** the H–F bond is over twice as polar, consistent with the larger electronegativity difference. Combined with the small size of F, this is why HF hydrogen bonds (b.p. 20 °C) while HCl does not (b.p. −85 °C).

### Example 3: explaining solubility

Explain why ethanoic acid is miscible with water, while ethyl ethanoate (CH₃COOCH₂CH₃) is only moderately soluble.

Ethanoic acid has an O–H group that can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water, and only a small non-polar part, so solute–water attractions replace the water–water hydrogen bonds well. Ethyl ethanoate has no O–H, so it can only accept hydrogen bonds through its oxygen lone pairs, and it has a larger hydrocarbon portion. The new attractions are weaker than the water–water hydrogen bonds lost, so solubility is limited.

## Common mistakes

- Saying that boiling breaks covalent bonds. Boiling a molecular substance only overcomes intermolecular forces.
- Calling any H atom in a molecule a hydrogen-bond donor. CH₄ and CH₃Cl cannot hydrogen bond: the H must be bonded to N, O or F.
- Assuming polar molecules always boil higher than non-polar ones. Large non-polar molecules (e.g. octane, b.p. 126 °C) boil higher than small polar ones because of dispersion.
- Treating a molecule with polar bonds as automatically polar. Check the shape: CO₂, BF₃ and CCl₄ are non-polar.
- Saying non-polar substances are "repelled" by water. They are insoluble because water–water hydrogen bonding is lost without compensation.

## Exam tips

- For any comparison, name every force present in each substance, then say which is stronger and why. Marks are for the reasoning, not the ranking alone.
- When dispersion forces decide the answer, mention number of electrons (or size) and shape (surface contact).
- Use the language "more energy is required to overcome the intermolecular forces" rather than "the bonds are stronger".
- Sketch hydrogen bonds with dashed lines, showing the lone pair and a near-linear X–H···Y arrangement.

## Key terms

- **Intermolecular force** — an electrostatic attraction between separate particles.
- **Electronegativity** — the tendency of an atom in a bond to attract the shared electrons.
- **Dipole moment** — a measure of molecular polarity, μ = Qr, in debye.
- **Ion–dipole force** — attraction between an ion and a polar molecule.
- **Hydration** — surrounding of a dissolved ion by water molecules.
- **Dipole–dipole force** — attraction between permanent dipoles of polar molecules.
- **Hydrogen bond** — attraction between H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on another N, O or F.
- **London dispersion force** — attraction between instantaneous and induced dipoles; present in all substances.
- **Polarisability** — how easily an electron cloud can be distorted.
- **Viscosity** — resistance of a fluid to flow.
- **Surface tension** — energy needed to increase the surface area of a liquid.

## Summary

- Intermolecular forces are electrostatic and much weaker than covalent or ionic bonds.
- Ion–dipole forces drive dissolving of salts; they are stronger for small, highly charged ions.
- Hydrogen bonding needs H on N, O or F plus a lone pair on N, O or F; it explains water's anomalously high boiling point.
- Dispersion forces exist in every substance and grow with electron number, size and surface contact; they can dominate for large molecules.
- Stronger intermolecular forces mean higher boiling point, viscosity and surface tension, and lower vapour pressure.
- Solubility depends on whether new solute–solvent attractions can replace those broken: "like dissolves like".

questions.prompt: Which of the following molecules can act as a hydrogen-bond donor in the pure liquid?
questions.explanation: A hydrogen-bond donor needs an H covalently bonded to N, O or F. Only CH₃NH₂ has this (N–H). B is tempting because it contains F, but its H atoms are bonded to C, not F. A and D have O lone pairs (so they can accept from water) but no O–H, so they cannot hydrogen bond to themselves.

options.A: attraction between permanent dipoles in polar molecules only
options.B: attraction between an ion and a polar molecule
options.C: the sharing of electron pairs between neighbouring molecules
options.D: attraction between instantaneous dipoles and the dipoles they induce in neighbouring particles

questions.explanation: Dispersion forces come from momentary uneven electron distributions that induce dipoles in neighbours; they act between all particles. A describes dipole–dipole forces, which is the common confusion; B is ion–dipole; C describes covalent bonding.

questions.prompt: HCl is more polar than HI, yet HI has the higher boiling point (−35 °C versus −85 °C). The best explanation is that:

options.A: HI has stronger dispersion forces because its larger electron cloud is more polarisable, and this outweighs the smaller dipole–dipole contribution
options.B: HI forms hydrogen bonds but HCl does not
options.C: the H–I covalent bond is stronger than the H–Cl bond
options.D: HI has a larger permanent dipole because iodine is more electronegative

questions.explanation: I has many more electrons than Cl, so HI is much more polarisable and its dispersion forces dominate. C is tempting but boiling does not break covalent bonds (and H–I is actually weaker). Iodine is less electronegative than chlorine (D), and neither forms hydrogen bonds (B).

questions.prompt: Pentane (b.p. 36 °C) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (b.p. 10 °C) are both C₅H₁₂. Why does pentane boil at a higher temperature?

options.A: Pentane is polar, while 2,2-dimethylpropane is non-polar.
options.B: Pentane has more electrons, giving stronger dispersion forces.
options.C: The long, unbranched shape of pentane gives a larger contact area between molecules, so dispersion forces are stronger.

questions.explanation: The isomers have the same number of electrons (so B is wrong), and both are essentially non-polar. The difference is shape: the compact, nearly spherical branched molecule touches neighbours over a smaller area, giving weaker dispersion forces. D wrongly links boiling to covalent bonds.

questions.prompt: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) is much more viscous than propan-1-ol. Which explanation is best?

options.A: Glycerol has three OH groups per molecule, so it forms more extensive hydrogen bonding that resists molecules sliding past one another.
options.B: Glycerol has a much higher molar mass, and viscosity depends only on molar mass.
options.C: Propan-1-ol is non-polar and has only dispersion forces.
options.D: Glycerol molecules are ionic in the liquid state.

questions.explanation: Each glycerol molecule can form several hydrogen bonds, building a network that strongly resists flow. B is tempting because size does affect viscosity, but molar mass alone does not decide it (and glycerol, 92 g mol⁻¹, is not vastly heavier than propan-1-ol, 60 g mol⁻¹). Propan-1-ol is polar and hydrogen bonds (C), and glycerol is molecular, not ionic (D).

questions.prompt: Which ion would you expect to have the most exothermic enthalpy of hydration?
questions.explanation: Ion–dipole attraction is strongest for ions with the highest charge density (high charge, small radius). Mg²⁺ has a 2+ charge and the smallest radius of these ions. C is tempting because it also has a 2+ charge, but Ca²⁺ is larger, so water molecules cannot approach as closely.

questions.prompt: HBr has a dipole moment of 0.82 D and a bond length of 141 pm. What is the approximate partial charge on each atom as a fraction of e? (1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m; e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.explanation: μ = 0.82 × 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ = 2.736 × 10⁻³⁰ C m. Q = μ/r = 2.736 × 10⁻³⁰ / 1.41 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 1.940 × 10⁻²⁰ C. Q/e = 1.940 × 10⁻²⁰ / 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 0.12. A and D come from a factor-of-ten slip when converting pm to m (141 pm = 1.41 × 10⁻¹⁰ m).

questions.prompt: Which substance is expected to be the most soluble in hexane, C₆H₁₄?
questions.explanation: Hexane is non-polar with only dispersion forces. I₂ is non-polar and highly polarisable, so I₂–hexane dispersion forces readily replace those broken, and it dissolves (giving a violet solution). C is tempting because methanol is small, but its hydrogen bonds to other methanol molecules are not replaced by anything comparable in hexane. NaCl and glucose need strong ion–dipole or hydrogen-bonding interactions.
